NO. 002 · Songbirds & City Birds / Passeridae · Sparrows

Eurasian Tree Sparrow

树麻雀 · shù má què Passer montanus
Resident Abundant 12–14 cm Protected (China) IUCN LC

The most overlooked — and most ubiquitous — of neighbours

The sparrow is too common to look at closely, which is why almost nobody does. Get near one and the design shows: a chestnut crown, snow-white cheeks and a small black bib. It is the most numerous bird in the cities of the Pearl River Delta, and the one that has worked out how to live with us.

Gallery

One scientific illustration for shape and colour blocks, two field photographs for how it looks in real light. Click any image to enlarge.

Identification

  • HeadChestnut crown, white cheeks, and a clear black ear-patch — that patch separates it from the House Sparrow.
  • ThroatBlack from throat to upper breast like a small bib, in sharp contrast with the white cheeks.
  • PlumageChestnut-brown back heavily streaked black; two white wingbars; buffy rump; dark brown tail.
  • SexesMale and female look alike (unlike House Sparrow), so they are hard to tell apart in the field.

Behaviour

Intensely sociable, feeding on the ground in hopping flocks of a dozen to a hundred and taking grain, grass seed, insects and human food scraps. Very alert: one bird flushes and the flock follows. Nests in wall cavities, roof tiles, air-conditioner holes and lamp housings, and will take over other birds' nest boxes. Dust-bathes enthusiastically on dry ground.

Voice

A thin, insistent 'cheep' — the baseline background noise of any southern Chinese city. The breeding song is slightly more structured but still a string of single notes.

Where to find it in Zhuhai

  • any inhabited street
  • around wet markets
  • Doumen rice paddies
  • bus stops
Field note
It is a protected species in China: catching or trading wild sparrows is illegal. Ordinary as it looks, it is load-bearing in the urban food web — the staple prey of hawks and shrikes.
